item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports attribute-sensitive representations, but provides limited direct evidence for a lightweight title/description encoder trained from scratch inside BERT4Rec. [MARS (CIKM 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00702) learns attribute-aware representations and attribute-wise user–item matching, motivating separate treatment of textual fields; its pretrained-language-model setting does not establish effectiveness without pretrained embeddings. [ConSRec (2024)](https://thesai.org/Publications/ViewPaper?Code=IJACSA&Issue=12&SerialNo=83&Volume=15) directly extends BERT4Rec with textual sentence representations, offering architectural precedent but not verified evidence here for jointly learned, randomly initialized text encoders. A task-compatible experimental hypothesis: pool trainable token embeddings separately for titles and descriptions, project and gate them into item-ID embeddings, and optimize the whole network through BERT4Rec’s masked-item objective. Compare against the corrected ID-only baseline; improvements remain unproven.\n\nComplementarity requires more than semantic similarity. [SComGNN (AAAI 2024)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28734) explicitly models both relevance and dissimilarity in complementary-item graphs, illustrating why similar-text retrieval can miss useful complements. Its graph-based evidence does not establish that purchase sequences identify compatibility, substitution, or fulfilled demand. With only histories, titles, descriptions and timestamps, treat such interpretations as hypotheses: metadata may expose product roles or compatibility terms, but observed next-item prediction provides indirect supervision. Test a jointly trained metadata branch within each single BERT4Rec model, using the fixed macro validation HR@10; avoid inferred relation labels or claims that a purchased item fulfilled a need."}
